paragraphs: Chaotic polarity reversals in a single magnetic vortex can provide both an irregular switching sequence and a programmable numerical probability. This study uses micromagnetic simulations of a field-driven Permalloy nanodisk to connect competing core-reversal mechanisms with irregular dwell times. Instead of equating the two core polarities with binary values, it encodes each dwell interval according to whether its duration exceeds a digital threshold. Changing that threshold tunes the proportion of output ones while leaving the magnetic drive unchanged, separating dynamical variability from probability calibration.

The resulting bitstream supplies the stochastic operand of a fractional multiplier. A second operand sets the number of gated positions, and counting produces the expected product after normalization by the full arithmetic window. The innovation is this combination of one chaotic oscillator, dwell-time encoding, and lightweight digital arithmetic. The contribution is a simulation-supported arithmetic proof of concept. Statistical tests cover a representative operating point, and the randomness benchmark uses separately post-processed data. Its significance lies in a possible compact route to programmable stochastic arithmetic, with experimental readout, energy cost, and broader accuracy benchmarks still to be demonstrated.

Twist-induced magnetic frustration can amplify a minute local perturbation into a different domain pattern without a continuously applied drive. Using micromagnetic simulations of twisted bilayer CrI3, this study traces that sensitivity to spatially alternating ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interlayer exchange. Competing interactions create many nearly degenerate domain configurations, so small initial-state changes redirect relaxation into different metastable states. The resulting chaos is transient: trajectories separate during texture formation and ultimately settle into static metastable patterns.

Across the sampled ensemble, domain occupancy variables are nearly unbiased and show no statistically detectable pairwise correlations. Further simulations find that selected patterns persist at low temperatures and dissolve with heating; a shuffled-coupling control shows that coherent moiré structure is essential to domain formation. The central innovation is spatially distributed, undriven magnetic basin sensitivity produced by an engineered exchange landscape. It broadens nonlinear magnetism from driven collective motion to the formation of interacting domains and suggests a route toward sampling magnetic configurations for unconventional computing. Turning this sampling concept into a device will require reproducible initialization and experimental tests of retention and readout.

Low crystal and interface symmetry can change the direction and character of electrically generated magnetic torques alongside their strength. This experimental study compares Permalloy coupled to WTe2 or MoTe2 with a Permalloy/Pt reference. Angle-resolved spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance separates the torque components, while Raman measurements characterize the reduced crystal symmetry. Both van der Waals heterostructures exhibit a field-like torque associated with out-of-plane spin polarization that is absent from the Pt reference. Its magnitude is comparable to the conventional damping-like torque generated by in-plane spin polarization.

Simulations using the measured torque efficiencies illustrate the dynamical consequence. The out-of-plane field-like torque initiates departure from an in-plane equilibrium, allowing the damping-like torque to sustain magnetization reversal without an applied magnetic field. The innovative element is identifying this torque symmetry experimentally and connecting it to a cooperative switching mechanism. The results place crystal and interface symmetry alongside spin Hall efficiency as design variables for controlling magnetization. Faster switching is a simulation result; the measurements do not uniquely distinguish spin-based from orbital-mediated origins of the unconventional torque.

The direction of an acoustic driving field determines whether it can exert the torque needed to excite magnetization. This study implements strain, lattice-rotation, and spin-rotation interactions in the mumax+ micromagnetic framework and uses them to separate the mechanisms of surface-acoustic-wave-driven ferromagnetic resonance. When the equilibrium magnetization is parallel to the wave propagation direction, the longitudinal magnetoelastic field produces no direct transverse torque. Lattice rotation instead supplies a transverse drive, explaining how resonance can persist where the conventional strain channel is geometrically suppressed.

Analytical angular dependences and simulations show how rotating the magnetization reactivates strain coupling and changes the balance between channels. Standing-wave calculations further connect the spatial magnetic response to rotation antinodes, providing a way to interpret location-dependent excitation. The innovation is a reusable implementation combined with a torque-based channel analysis that distinguishes strain amplitude from excitation efficiency. It offers a framework for designing acoustic control experiments and testing residual absorption near longitudinal alignment. The calculations prescribe the elastic wave and neglect magnetic back-action; strong-coupling estimates concern enhanced, adjustable rotation-coupling strengths, so applying them to ordinary yttrium iron garnet requires material-specific validation.

Self-consistent photon and magnetization dynamics can be modeled within a micromagnetic framework without solving the full electromagnetic field. This study extends mumax+ by coupling cavity-mode amplitudes to magnetic precession and returning the cavity field to the magnet. A Python co-simulation implementation reproduces the transition between unresolved resonances and hybridized magnon-photon modes, including coherent energy exchange. With multiple cavity modes, the model captures indirect energy transfer through a shared magnon, while spatial overlap determines whether a cavity profile couples to the uniform magnetic mode.

The framework explores how dissipative coupling changes level repulsion into level attraction and provides an illustrative antiferromagnetic extension with separate tracking of the two sublattices. These benchmarks connect numerical behavior to analytical coupled-mode models and establish a tool for prototyping hybrid magnetic resonators. Its computational innovation is a two-tier design: an accessible Python route and CUDA kernels designed for simultaneous integration and spatially resolved coupling. The published benchmarks use the Python tier; the native tier still requires build integration. The framework is classical, and its antiferromagnetic example uses parameters chosen for a microwave-frequency demonstration; extensions to realistic high-frequency antiferromagnets require material-specific validation.

Spin–orbit torques from AuPt can electrically excite thickness-quantized spin waves in a single GdFeCo layer. Using spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance, this study resolves the uniform resonance and perpendicular standing modes up to the third order. Ta-capped films retain higher-order modes, consistent with oxidation suppression and stronger boundary pinning. Uncapped films show less stable magnetic properties, weaker pinning, and a reduced set of observable modes.

Microscopy, elemental mapping, and element-specific magnetic measurements connect the spectral changes to film chemistry, while resonance analysis and micromagnetic calculations support the confinement interpretation. The key design lesson is that passivation and interfaces help determine which magnetic modes an electrical current can address. Although GdFeCo is ferrimagnetic, the measurements probe an effectively ferromagnetic dynamical regime, away from compensation. The work establishes an experimental basis for engineering electrically driven multimode spin dynamics through controlled materials preparation and motivates future memory and logic designs that exploit controlled mode excitation.

Rotating magnetic fields provide a route from geometric vortex motion to deterministic chaos. Zero-temperature micromagnetic simulations of confined Permalloy vortices and antivortices reveal regular, multi-lobed trajectories under weak driving. A trochoidal constant relates the drive frequency and core polarity to the orbit’s rotational symmetry and closure sequence. Chirality changes the starting phase, while polarity and field rotation determine the orbital geometry. This description connects the shape of a magnetic trajectory to the competing intrinsic and externally imposed rotations.

Stronger excitation destabilizes the regular motion and produces repeated, irregular reversals of the vortex core. Maps of the largest Lyapunov exponent and trajectories from nearly identical initial states distinguish chaotic switching from locked or quasi-periodic behavior. Field amplitude and frequency also bias the time-averaged polarity, giving control over the switching statistics. The central finding is a tunable connection between orbital geometry and binary core reversal in a compact magnetic texture. It motivates field-driven elements for probabilistic or reservoir computing, with device performance requiring experimental validation.

Probabilistic computing can represent choices among several groups directly through fluctuating units with more than two states. This study develops a geometric extension of binary probabilistic bits to multilevel units and applies it to number partitioning: distributing numbers among groups whose sums should be balanced. The formulation combines tunable state probabilities with problem-dependent interactions, allowing three-way and five-way assignments within a common framework. Its innovation is an explicit multilevel update rule that connects stochastic state selection to an optimization objective.

Binary simulations informed by measured magnetic-tunnel-junction fluctuations examine how annealing schedules influence exploration, trapping, and solution quality. Multilevel simulations then show a preference for well-balanced partitions, using software-generated randomness. The results emphasize that the timing of probability bias matters alongside the representation of the problem. They also show that useful low-cost configurations can coexist with imperfect convergence to the optimum. The work offers a basis for multilevel probabilistic optimization and identifies candidate physical implementations, while hardware realization and computational advantage remain open questions.

The Pd/Co interface can generate a field-like spin–orbit torque stronger than its damping-like counterpart. Measurements find a field-like torque efficiency roughly 20–40 times larger than in the studied Pd/CoFe and Pd/Permalloy bilayers. Spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance and harmonic Hall measurements independently support the enhancement. The result makes the identity of the magnetic interface a central control variable for torque generation, even when the heavy-metal layer is unchanged.

Analysis of damping, surface anisotropy, and spin-mixing conductance links the large torque to interfacial spin–orbit coupling and associated spin transport. Interfacial spin loss and additional damping channels materially alter the inferred spin transparency. Micromagnetic simulations using experimentally informed parameters further predict faster in-plane magnetization reversal for Pd/Co and show a strong dependence on the field-like torque. The innovation is to treat this torque as a useful switching resource whose strength can be engineered at the interface. These results motivate torque-balanced memory and logic designs; the reported switching benefit is a numerical prediction, and the microscopic interfacial mechanism warrants further investigation.

A single confined skyrmion can serve as a reconfigurable logic element when its nonlinear response is controlled through magnetic anisotropy. Micromagnetic simulations show that periodic modulation of perpendicular anisotropy produces both ordered and strongly initial-state-sensitive sequences of topological charge, including polarity reversal and annihilation. The study uses this sensitivity to encode different logic functions in the initial skyrmion configuration. Spin–orbit torques prepare that configuration, while four modulation amplitudes represent the four combinations of two binary inputs.

A mapping of initial conditions realizes all sixteen two-input Boolean truth tables in the simulated nanodisk. Every function uses the same output criterion: the relaxed final state determines whether the output is true or false. Grouping neighboring initial conditions that produce the same truth table creates operating windows for selecting each function. The central innovation is a common magnetic element whose function changes through preparation, with a fixed readout rule and modulation duration. The work proposes a route toward voltage-controlled, field-free logic and identifies initial-state control as a design requirement; practical noise tolerance and energy savings require device-level validation.

This study links chaotic skyrmion motion to feedback between internal deformation and orbital motion. Micromagnetic simulations of a skyrmion confined in a Co/Pt nanodisk show that excitation of the higher gyrotropic mode couples orbital rotation to a nonuniform, breathing-like distortion. The changing shape modifies the skyrmion's effective inertia and restoring force, producing intricate hypotrochoidal trajectories rather than a simple rigid-body orbit.

By combining trajectory geometry, bifurcation diagrams, sensitivity to initial conditions, and local Lyapunov analysis, the study maps how the dynamics evolve with both drive strength and elapsed time. Increasing the oscillating field produces fixed-point, periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic regimes, with strong driving eventually destabilizing the skyrmion. Crucially, the same drive can pass through different dynamical stages during a single evolution, so an initial regular trajectory does not guarantee a regular long-term response.

The contribution is a physical explanation and diagnostic framework for field-driven skyrmion chaos. It identifies conditions relevant to reliable magnetic operation and suggests how deterministic sensitivity might support future chaos-based computing. Computing functionality and experimental realization remain prospective; the reported evidence is numerical.

The magnetic response of a magnetosome assembly depends on interactions between neighboring chains, not only on the properties of individual nanoparticles. This study combines experiments and finite-element micromagnetic simulations to explain how biologically produced magnetite particles reverse their magnetization after being organized into linear arrays. Magnetosomes extracted from magnetotactic bacteria were deposited under an applied magnetic field, producing aligned chains with a magnetic easy axis along their length. Higher particle concentrations produced denser assemblies with lower coercivity.

Angular hysteresis measurements indicate that an assembly does not reverse as one uniformly rotating magnetic object. The simulations resolve the underlying sequence: reversed magnetization nucleates in selected particles, often near chain ends or outer corners, and spreads through successive particle switching. Changing the number of chains or their separation alters the dipolar fields, the nucleation pattern, and the field required for reversal.

The advance is the connection between experimentally controlled assembly geometry and the microscopic reversal mechanism. It establishes chain packing as a practical variable for tailoring the magnetic response of these biogenic nanoparticles. The results provide guidance for designing magnetosome-based magnetic materials and motivate future studies of their biomedical applications.

Recursive geometry can generate a corresponding hierarchy of magnetic excitations. This study designs magnonic crystals by superimposing progressively smaller antidot lattices in a Permalloy film and uses micromagnetic simulations to examine the resulting spin-wave modes. As the fractal construction advances, ordinary edge and channel modes split into doublets, triplets, and quintets. Their spatial patterns inherit the same recursive organization as the underlying arrangement of holes.

The mechanism is the asymmetric internal magnetic-energy landscape created by the overlapping lattices. Local demagnetizing fields distinguish regions that were equivalent in a simpler array, splitting their resonances and confining modes to different parts of the structure. Comparison with a symmetric, nonfractal array containing two hole sizes shows that multiple sizes alone do not reproduce the splitting. At the smallest modeled spacing, exchange and dipolar interactions also hybridize edge and channel excitations. Geometry and applied bias fields can reduce the asymmetry, bringing separated modes together or changing their ordering.

The innovation is a geometrical route to organizing both resonance frequencies and their locations within a magnetic film. These simulation results identify recursive geometry and bias fields as variables for designing selectively addressable magnonic oscillators, sensors, and memory elements.

Curvature provides an additional way to stabilize and manipulate magnetic skyrmions. Finite-element micromagnetic simulations of ultrathin hemispherical shells show how shell size, surface-normal anisotropy, and intrinsic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction select vortex, skyrmion, skyrmionium, or surface-normal magnetic states. The curvature-induced interaction favors one skyrmion chirality while opposing the other, unlike the more symmetric behavior of a flat disk. For sufficiently curved shells and suitable anisotropy, a skyrmion can remain stable even without intrinsic Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.

The study also resolves how these curved textures respond dynamically. Alongside gyration and breathing modes, coupling to azimuthal spin waves produces more complex core trajectories. Resonant excitation of breathing modes enables conversion between skyrmion and skyrmionium states. A two-stage conversion can reverse the skyrmion's core polarity through a transient skyrmionium, with each drive selected to excite the relevant texture. Switching maps identify the field strengths and frequencies that support these transitions.

The contribution links geometry-controlled stability to a specific resonant switching mechanism. It suggests a route toward magnetic memory elements controlled by geometry and resonant excitation. The modeled shell system provides specific stability and switching conditions to test in future experiments.
